props.title: Go West

sections.content: Buster Keaton's Go West stands as one of his most emotionally resonant works, trading his typical mechanical precision for surprising tenderness. Unlike the frenetic energy of The General (1926) or Steamboat Bill Jr. (1928), this film follows "Friendless" - Keaton's character - forming an unlikely bond with Brown Eyes the cow in an otherwise hostile frontier environment. The film brilliantly subverts Western tropes while maintaining Keaton's trademark physical comedy, particularly in the climactic cattle drive through Los Angeles that turns city streets into chaos.

sections.content: Go West marked a fascinating shift in silent comedy's approach to the Western genre. While earlier films like The Paleface (1922) played frontier life purely for laughs, Keaton incorporated genuine pathos and commentary on isolation in the American West. His character's inability to connect with humans, finding companionship only with a cow, offers surprising depth beneath the comedy. This approach influenced later Western comedies like Way Out West (1937) with Laurel and Hardy.

The film's technical achievements deserve special note. Keaton's signature long shots and practical stunts reach new heights in the cattle drive sequence. Unlike the mechanical precision of The Navigator (1924) or the train sequences in The General (1926), handling hundreds of cattle through actual Los Angeles streets required a different kind of choreography. This blending of urban and frontier environments predates similar juxtapositions in films like City Slickers (1991) by decades. SUBHEAD: Silent Comedy Meets The Western

sections.content: The fusion of silent comedy with Western elements created a unique hybrid that influenced decades of filmmaking. While Go West played with genre expectations, it maintained authentic Western elements that would later appear in straight Westerns like The Great Train Robbery (1903) and Stagecoach (1939). Keaton's ability to find humor in frontier hardship while respecting the setting's inherent drama created a template for later comedy-Westerns like Blazing Saddles (1974).
